newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-It is always political season in New Hampshire.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-It is always political season in New Hampshire.

text.p: The next U.S. presidential election is more than 900 days away, but that has not kept politicians from coming to New Hampshire in the middle of black fly season.

They show up in this state, which every four years holds the nation's first presidential primary, not to declare that they are running for president but to announce that they have not yet made up their minds.
On the Republican side, New Hapmshire residents have been able to recently see millionaire flat-taxer Steve Forbes, Sen. John McCain of Arizona and Sen. Don Nickles of Oklahoma.
Former Tennessee Gov. Lamar Alexander keeps reporters for the state's newspapers, TV and radio stations appraised of his latest views by fax.
Democrat Richard Gephardt, the House Minority Leader, has visited twice this year and Vice President Al Gore is slated to tour the state on May 27 starting in Nashua.
Each politician during this cold, wet spring that has spawned a black fly plague has denied the visits were politically inspired.
"The future will take care of itself," huffed Gephardt when asked about his plans for the 2000 primary at his first stop in the state in April.

Last weekend at a Bedford fund-raiser -- the Hillsborough County Democratic Committee's Presidential Awards dinner -- the Missouri Democrat told reporters he had not decided whether to run for president in 2000.
NOT RUNNING YET
"I'm really on the issues in front of us in Congress and I'm working hard to win a majority in 1998," Gephardt said.
Patrick Kennedy, a Rhode Island Democratic congressman, was also at the dinner and told reporters that if Gephardt were to run, "He's got my full support."
Forbes also dodged the question after a recent speech before prominent New Hampshire women Republicans in Windham.

The coyness prompted chuckles from veteran primary observers. Black flies, which thrive in cool wet conditions, are the bane of northern New England each spring. They are blood-feeders, and their bites are painful. In addition, many people are allergic to a compound in the black fly's saliva and end up with huge, red welts.

"No person who is sane would hang around black fly season talking about politics if they didn't plan to run," laughed state GOP party chairman Steve Duprey when asked to comment on the flurry of "unofficial visits."
"Steve Forbes would not be hanging around New Hampshire this time of year if he wasn't planning to run. That's my take on it," echoed Jeff Woodburn, state Democratic Party Committee chairman.

Magazine publisher Forbes, a fourth place finisher in the 1996 Republican presidential primary, has been a frequent caller to New Hampshire radio talk shows and recently made a one-day swing through the state visiting top Republicans.
"I have to make a decision late next year whether I am going to run in 2000," Forbes said.

"In the meantime, I have launched an organisation called Americans for Hope, Growth and Opportunity to pinpoint issues like the flat tax or parental control of schools so regardless of who does emerge in the year 2000 they will be responding to this positive agenda."
FORBES VIEWS GET A FEW HEADLINES

The state chapter of Americans for Hope, Growth and Opportunity has been issuing Forbes' views on social security reform and retirement accounts for young workers. Forbes' blast condemning Senate Democrats' bill providing exemptions for the partial birth abortion garnered a few New Hampshire headlines.
Meanwhile, Gephardt has logged two visits to the state already this year. But the Missouri Democrat continues to insist his forays are to recruit candidates for the 1998 congressional elections.
So far Forbes has drawn the most press attention and fuelled early speculation.
"He is very impressive ... he talks in those optimistic tones like Ronald Reagan did. People like a candidate who talks about the future with optimism. They want to have hope," Duprey said.
